findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build downloads and executes whatever content this URL serves. A compromised origin, redirected endpoint, or altered release can run arbitrary code in the build environment and embed it in the produced image; there is no version or checksum to make the artifact reproducible or trustworthy.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Every build executes whatever content the URL serves at build time. The script is neither version-pinned nor checksum/signature-verified, so a compromised or changed upstream endpoint can execute arbitrary code in the build and silently alter the produced image.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: This downloads mutable network content and immediately executes it during the image build. A compromised endpoint, DNS/proxy path, or changed script can run arbitrary commands in the build environment and produce a malicious image; there is no immutable version, checksum, or signature verification.

findings.title: Make a failed installer download fail the image build
findings.whyItBreaks: If curl fails before writing output (for example, a DNS or connection failure), the pipeline status is sh's status. BusyBox sh succeeds on empty input, so Docker reports a successful build even though the intended installation never occurred.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key status in the new public loader
findings.whyItBreaks: Discarding ErrMissing makes an absent key indistinguishable from a present key whose value is "". The exported API forces all callers to treat a failed lookup as valid data, unlike Load which exposes ErrMissing.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported wrapper discards it and returns "". Callers therefore cannot distinguish lookup failure from a key deliberately stored with an empty string.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported API discards it and returns "". Callers cannot distinguish a missing key from a key intentionally stored with an empty value.

findings.title: Preserve completion before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send is detached into a goroutine, so Run can return before any result is delivered. Previously every send completed before return. A caller that closes results after Run returns will now race with these goroutines and can panic with "send on closed channel"; callers also cannot rely on returned results being complete.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run returned only after every value had been sent. It now returns immediately after launching goroutines. A valid caller sequence of Run(...); close(results) can therefore close the channel while a launched goroutine executes `results <- j * 2`, causing a `send on closed channel` panic; callers that do not close it can also observe incomplete results when Run returns.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each job is sent from an untracked goroutine, so Run returns before any or all results are delivered. A caller that treats Run returning as completion can observe missing results or close results and cause the remaining goroutines to panic on send.

findings.title: Keep record deletion limited to same-tenant admins
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || makes canDeleteRecord return true for a non-admin in the same tenant and for an admin in a different tenant. Both cases were rejected by the prior authorization policy, so either can delete records outside the intended admin-and-tenant boundary.

findings.title: Require admin and tenant match before deleting records
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing && with || makes canDeleteRecord return true for any non-admin session whose tenantId matches the record. Those users can now delete records despite isAdmin=false.

findings.title: Require admin status and tenant match for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || authorizes a non-admin whenever their tenant matches the record, and authorizes an admin for records in another tenant. Either case bypasses the prior requirement that deletion needs both privileges.

findings.title: Preserve invalid-settings errors instead of overwriting with defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or schema-invalid settings previously stopped updateFontSize before save. They now become DEFAULTS, so updateFontSize writes a new record with theme "light" and the requested size, silently replacing the existing invalid/corrupt settings and erasing any recoverable value such as a valid non-default theme.

findings.title: Do not overwrite invalid settings with defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or schema-invalid stored settings previously threw from parseSettings before updateFontSize reached save. They now become { theme: "light", fontSize: 14 }, so updateFontSize overwrites the invalid/incompatible stored value with defaults and the requested size. The caller cannot distinguish recovery from a legitimate settings value.

findings.title: Propagate invalid-settings failures instead of saving defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: For malformed JSON or invalid fields, parseSettings now returns a valid-looking default object rather than signaling failure. updateFontSize then changes its fontSize and calls save, so input such as "{" now saves {"theme":"light","fontSize":18}; before this change the parse error prevented that write.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the reported branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` is resolved from the requested `branch`, but `artifacts` are always read from the unrelated `verified` ref. For example, a report for `feature` can claim it was built from commit A while listing artifacts from verified commit B.

findings.title: Use the requested branch commit for artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", builtFrom names the requested branch commit while artifacts are fetched from the verified commit. The report is internally inconsistent and returns the wrong artifact set.

findings.title: Read artifacts from the requested branch
findings.whyItBreaks: When branch and verified resolve to different commits, builtFrom contains the requested branch commit while artifacts contains artifacts from verified. The report therefore misattributes artifacts to the wrong build.

findings.title: Restore slicing to the requested limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, recentEntries now returns every entry rather than at most limit. renderFeed relies on its 20-entry request: with 21 inputs, its loop writes index 20, extending the allocated array and returning 21 entries.

findings.title: Apply the requested entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns every reversed entry rather than at most limit entries. renderFeed calls it with 20 at src/feed.ts:9, then iterates page.length, so feeds with more than 20 entries extend its initially sized array and are returned unbounded.

findings.title: Restore enforcement of the requested entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, this returns every reversed entry instead of at most limit entries. For example, renderFeed passes 20 at src/feed.ts:9; with 21 entries, its loop writes page[20], extending the intended 20-element result to 21 entries.

findings.title: Report the number of emitted manifest rows
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry has stale=true, its row is removed but the unchanged header call still supplies entries.length. The resulting # entry-count claims more entries than the manifest contains, causing consumers that use the header to miscount or reject the artifact.

findings.title: Count only entries emitted in the manifest
findings.whyItBreaks: With one live and one stale entry, this change emits one data row but retains `# entry-count: 2` because the header still receives `entries.length`. Consumers relying on the header to determine the number of manifest rows will see a malformed manifest.

findings.title: Count only rows that remain in the manifest
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, its row is omitted but the header still receives entries.length, so `# entry-count` overstates the number of manifest rows. Consumers relying on the header to parse or validate the manifest will see an inconsistent document.

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported FormatLegacyID symbol makes existing consumers fail to compile when upgrading, and removes their ability to generate the persisted/external LEG########## identifier format.

findings.title: Restore the removed legacy formatter API
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing exported FormatLegacyID makes downstream users of the ids package fail to compile on upgrade. The deleted test demonstrates the established LEG-prefixed, 10-digit formatting contract; deleting it also removes the only in-repository compatibility check.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: Consumers importing shippingQuote from src/orders can no longer compile after upgrading, although this module previously exported that function.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is exported with a string return contract, but this changed line unconditionally throws. Every consumer now receives an exception rather than the prior uppercase string result.

findings.title: Restore execute’s string-returning behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is exported with a string return type, but this implementation synchronously throws for every input. Consumers can no longer receive the transformed string that the prior implementation returned.

findings.title: Return the declared string result
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the public execute(input: string): string API now throws before producing a string, regressing the previous uppercase result for all inputs.

findings.title: Preserve the read-only viewer handling path
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer with fewer than five attempts, this new guard makes isEligible return false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24. Before this change, that same request passed eligibility and reached the explicit "read-only" result at line 25.

findings.title: Allow viewers to reach the read-only handler path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer below the attempt limit now fails isEligible and handle returns "rejected" at line 24. The following viewer branch, which returns "read-only", can therefore never run.

findings.title: Preserve active viewer read-only handling
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer below the attempt limit now fails isEligible and handle returns "rejected" at line 24. Previously it reached line 25 and returned "read-only", so that explicitly supported role-specific outcome is unreachable.

findings.title: Keep unpaid drafts saveable
findings.whyItBreaks: For { state: "draft", payment: "missing" }, canProceed now returns false, so saveDraft returns "blocked". Saving a draft is distinct from submitting an order and should not require payment.

findings.title: Keep unpaid drafts saveable
findings.whyItBreaks: For `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }`, `canProceed` now returns false. `saveDraft` therefore returns "blocked" instead of "saved", even though payment status does not govern persisting a draft.

findings.title: Keep saving drafts independent of payment
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` shares `canProceed`; therefore `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }` now returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Payment status may govern submission, but it should not prevent persisting a draft.

findings.title: Read files from the returned snapshot commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel other than "stable", the returned Snapshot.commit is repo.headCommit(channel) while Snapshot.files is read from repo.headCommit("stable"). Consumers therefore receive a self-inconsistent snapshot and can publish or inspect stable's files while labeling them as the requested channel's commit.

findings.title: Read files from the snapshot commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot reports commit=repo.headCommit(channel) but files from repo.headCommit("stable"). Consumers therefore receive a self-inconsistent snapshot and can attribute stable's files to the requested channel commit.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: The snapshot reports `commit` as `repo.headCommit(channel)`, but its `files` now come from `repo.headCommit("stable")`. Publishing any channel whose head differs from `stable` therefore returns files that do not match the advertised commit or channel.

findings.title: Apply the requested limit
findings.whyItBreaks: `build("item", 2)` still returns ten entries because the implementation continues to loop over the hard-coded `max_count = 10`. The public parameter promises a result cap but has no observable effect.

findings.title: Honor the requested limit
findings.whyItBreaks: build(prefix, limit=3) accepts a caller-specified result limit but line 2 still hardcodes max_count = 10, returning ten items regardless of the supplied limit.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=3)` still returns ten entries because the loop reads the unchanged hard-coded `max_count = 10`. The public parameter therefore promises observable output capping that the implementation does not provide.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int("-1") returns -1 and its caller charge then returns -100 cents. This contradicts the new public name's positive-only contract and permits invalid negative or zero charges.

findings.title: Validate the promised positive integer
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int("0") and parse_positive_int("-1") return 0 and -1 rather than rejecting them. charge therefore permits a zero or negative charge (for example, "-1" becomes -100), contradicting the public helper's positive-only contract.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name promises a positive integer, but int(value) accepts zero and negatives. Consequently, charge("-1") accepts the invalid amount and produces -100 cents rather than rejecting it.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation modified a defensive copy. This version writes directly into df, so callers that retain or discard the returned value will observe their original DataFrame changed.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's input DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation copied df and updated the copy. This now writes through df.loc and returns the same object, so callers that retain the original DataFrame observe their source data unexpectedly overwritten.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation copied df before applying updates. The new implementation writes through to the supplied DataFrame, so callers that retain df for later use unexpectedly observe its value column changed.

findings.title: Keep the CI workflow under .github/workflows
findings.whyItBreaks: This rename removes the repository's only file from .github/workflows. GitHub Actions will treat docs/ci.md as documentation rather than a workflow, so pushes and pull requests no longer run npm ci, lint, or tests.

findings.title: Keep the CI definition under .github/workflows
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub Actions only discovers workflow YAML files in .github/workflows. This rename removes the repository's only workflow from that directory, so lint and tests will no longer run on push or pull requests.

findings.title: Restore the CI workflow under .github/workflows
findings.whyItBreaks: This rename removes the repository’s only .github/workflows entry. GitHub Actions discovers workflow YAML files only in .github/workflows, so the push and pull_request triggers in this file will no longer run; README.md:5 consequently makes a false claim.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in `parse_positive_int`
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name promises a positive result, but `s.parse()` accepts signed integers: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns -1. The current `charge` consumer consequently produces -100 for that input.

findings.title: Preserve the removed `read_int` public API
findings.whyItBreaks: Renaming a `pub fn` removes `read_int` outright. Existing consumers importing or calling that exported symbol will fail to compile after upgrading.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name promises a positive integer, but parsing "-7" returns -7 and parsing "0" returns 0. charge then trusts this contract and returns a negative or zero charge rather than rejecting the invalid amount.

findings.title: Reject non-positive input in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name promises a positive integer, but `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` returns negative inputs unchanged. Consequently, `charge("-1")` produces `-100`, allowing a negative charge through the newly named positive-only path.

findings.title: Preserve `items` after debug logging
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items);` evaluates and returns the owned `Vec<String>`, then the statement drops that returned value. The subsequent `items.len()` uses a moved value, producing Rust error E0382 and blocking compilation.

findings.title: Borrow items when printing debug output
findings.whyItBreaks: dbg!(items) evaluates and moves the Vec<String>; its returned value is discarded. The items.len() call on line 3 therefore borrows a moved value, causing Rust error E0382 and blocking compilation.

findings.title: Borrow items before debugging it
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` takes ownership of the `Vec<String>` and its returned value is discarded at the statement semicolon. The subsequent `items.len()` therefore uses a moved value, causing Rust error E0382 and preventing compilation.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the reported revision
findings.whyItBreaks: `fromRevision` remains the resolved pinned tag, but `changedPaths` is computed from `latest`. Consumers replaying this changeset atop `fromRevision`, as its public contract specifies, receive paths for a different revision.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the pinned revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When `pinnedTag` resolves to a revision other than `latest`, `fromRevision` identifies the pinned revision but `changedPaths` describes changes relative to `latest`. Consumers replaying those paths on `fromRevision`, as the exported Changeset contract requires, receive a mismatched changeset.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the declared base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When pinnedTag resolves differently from "latest", changedPaths is computed from latest while fromRevision remains the pinned revision. Consumers therefore replay a changeset whose paths were derived from a different base, yielding missed or incorrect changes.

findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users no longer has an email column, but src/query.sql:1 still executes SELECT email FROM users. That query will fail after upgrade instead of returning user contact data.

findings.title: Update queries to use contact_email
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration runs, users.email no longer exists, but src/query.sql:1 still executes SELECT email FROM users. That query will fail with a missing-column error on upgraded databases.

findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users no longer has an email column, but src/query.sql:1 still executes SELECT email FROM users. Any path using that query will fail with a missing-column database error.

findings.title: Restore environment-sourced billing credentials
findings.whyItBreaks: This commits a `bk_live_` billing key to repository history, exposing it to every repository reader and any distributed artifact. It also replaces the per-deployment `BILLING_API_KEY`, so key rotation and environment-specific billing accounts are silently ignored.

findings.title: Remove the committed live billing API key
findings.whyItBreaks: A credential marked as live is embedded in source control and returned by every deployment. Anyone with repository access can extract and use it, and all environments are forced to share that credential.

findings.title: Preserve failure when billing configuration is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: makeClient is exported, but it no longer signals that BILLING_API_KEY is absent. Callers receive a seemingly valid client using the committed key, so configuration failures are silently conflated with a valid production configuration.

findings.title: Remove the hard-coded live billing key
findings.whyItBreaks: This exposes a production-style API credential to everyone with repository access and makes every deployment use that credential, ignoring its configured BILLING_API_KEY. The prior missing-key failure is also removed, so misconfigured environments silently send billing traffic with the committed key.

findings.title: Restore handling for a missing settings file
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() returns None when path does not exist (line 7). The deleted fallback previously supplied default workers; startup() now subscripts None and raises TypeError instead of returning the default worker count.

findings.title: Restore handling for a missing settings file
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). startup now subscripts that None value, raising TypeError instead of preserving the prior default worker count of 1.

findings.title: Preserve startup behavior when the settings file is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist (lines 6-7). startup now indexes that None value, raising TypeError instead of using the previous one-worker default.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge only logs it and returns nil. Callers therefore cannot distinguish a failed charge from a successful one and may mark an unpaid transaction as paid.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the error then returns nil. This exported API now conflates a declined/failed charge with a successful one, so callers may fulfill an order or record payment despite no charge being submitted.

findings.title: Propagate the gateway submission failure
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit rejects a charge, Charge logs the error and returns nil. Callers therefore treat an unprocessed payment as successful and cannot retry or surface the failure.

findings.title: Include tenantId in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Calling settingsFor("tenant-a", "theme") caches under "settings:theme". A later settingsFor("tenant-b", "theme") hits that entry at line 13 and returns tenant-a's value without calling store.fetch, causing cross-tenant settings disclosure and incorrect configuration.

findings.title: Preserve the invalidate tenantId parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported function previously accepted invalidate(tenantId, name). Existing TypeScript consumers now fail to compile with two arguments; JavaScript consumers silently treat tenantId as name and delete "settings:<tenantId>", leaving the intended setting cached.

findings.title: Include tenantId in the cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A fetches a setting named `name`, this caches it as `settings:name`. A later `settingsFor(tenantB, name, store)` returns tenant A's value without calling the tenant B store, disclosing or misapplying tenant-scoped configuration.

findings.title: Retain invalidate's tenant argument
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported TypeScript API previously required `invalidate(tenantId, name)`. Existing consumers compiled against the prior version now fail with an excess-argument error when upgrading, with no compatibility overload or migration path.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The process-wide cache now keys only on name. After tenant A caches a setting named "theme", tenant B's settingsFor call for "theme" returns tenant A's cached value at line 14 and never invokes its tenant-specific store.fetch call.

findings.title: Keep the existing synchronous reserve contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, callers could branch directly on the boolean result. An async function always returns a truthy Promise, so existing JavaScript such as `if (inventory.reserve("sold-out"))` now permits the action although the Promise resolves to false; TypeScript callers also no longer type-check.

findings.title: Preserve no-argument Inventory construction
findings.whyItBreaks: The previously valid `new Inventory()` now leaves `store` undefined in existing JavaScript consumers. Reserving available stock then produces a rejected Promise when line 17 evaluates `this.store.save`, turning the former working in-memory path into a failure.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: `await` yields before line 18 updates `stock`. With one unit loaded, two `reserve(sku)` calls started before either Promise resolves both read `remaining === 1`, both save 0, and both resolve true. Two customers are therefore told they reserved the sole unit.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: The await creates an interleaving point before local stock is decremented. With stock=1, two concurrent reserve calls both read 1, both save 0, and both return true, resulting in two successful reservations for one item.

findings.title: Serialize reservations across the persistence await
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two calls to reserve(sku) can both read remaining=1 before either awaited save resumes. Both persist 0 and both return true, so two reservations succeed for one unit. The former synchronous implementation updated stock before another call could observe the old value.

findings.title: Preserve the published Inventory API or provide a migration
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, consumers could construct `new Inventory()` and use the synchronous boolean result of `reserve`. The required Store constructor argument now breaks TypeScript callers, while JavaScript callers fail at `undefined.save`; existing conditional callers such as `if (inventory.reserve(sku))` instead see a truthy Promise even when the reservation eventually resolves false.

findings.title: Update retry to consume millisecond backoff values
findings.whyItBreaks: `retry` still calls `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. For attempt 0, the changed function returns 1,000, so a failed operation waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 minutes) instead of 1,000 ms; later retries can wait up to 30,000 seconds.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 ms, but retry still multiplies it by 1,000 before passing it to sleep. A retry after its first failed attempt therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16m40s) instead of 1 second; later waits can reach about 8.3 hours.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, and schedulePoll was updated accordingly. retry() still multiplies that result by 1,000 at src/jobs/retry.ts:12, so its first retry waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 minutes) instead of the previous 1,000 ms; later retries are likewise 1,000x too slow.

findings.title: Return the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is ignored. After a successful buffered flush, a close failure is now returned as nil, so callers are told the save succeeded even when final file completion reports an error. The previous implementation returned this error.

findings.title: Return the close error after a successful flush
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. A final write/close failure after a successful buffer flush therefore makes Save return nil, so callers cannot distinguish a completed save from a failed one. Previously this error was returned.

findings.title: Return an error from f.Close
findings.whyItBreaks: When Flush succeeds but f.Close fails, Save now returns nil because the deferred Close result is ignored. Previously that failure was returned to Save's caller, so callers could detect an incomplete or failed write.

findings.title: Include the final row in page windows
findings.whyItBreaks: `_window_bounds` returns a half-open `[start, end)` interval, but `range(start, end - 1)` excludes `end - 1`. Every nonempty page loses its final row; a page size of one produces an empty page. `render_page` and `summarize` therefore omit rows.

findings.title: Include the final row in each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: The half-open bounds end is excluded again with `end - 1`, so each page loses its last row; a one-row page becomes empty and summarize/render_page omit records.

findings.title: Include the final row in every page
findings.whyItBreaks: `end` is already an exclusive bound; subtracting one makes every nonempty window omit its last row. Consequently `render_page` and `summarize` silently omit records, and a page size of one renders no rows.

findings.title: Preserve existing keyword-call compatibility
findings.whyItBreaks: The non-private module functions no longer accept their established keyword arguments (`n`/`lo`/`hi`, `total`/`size`, and `page`/`size`). Existing callers using those documented-by-signature keywords now fail with `TypeError` before pagination runs.

findings.title: Return cache entries only before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has elapsed time below ttlMs, so this condition is false and get() deletes it and returns null. Once an entry is expired, the condition becomes true and get() returns the stale value indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice the array while iterating forward
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item shifts the next item into the current index, but forEach advances to the next index. For `[done, done]`, the first job is removed and the second is skipped, so pruneDone returns a completed job. This also changes the prior non-mutating filter contract by modifying the caller's array.

findings.title: Keep valid entries until their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: An entry read immediately after set has an age near zero, so the new `>` condition deletes it and returns null. Conversely, entries older than `ttlMs` are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Remove all completed jobs without skipping adjacent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing while `forEach` advances its index skips the element shifted into the removed slot. For `[done, done, pending]`, the second done job remains in the returned queue. This also changes the prior non-mutating API behavior.

findings.title: Return entries only before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly set entry has age near zero, so it is deleted and reported absent. Once its age exceeds ttlMs, the expired value is returned indefinitely instead.

findings.title: Remove every completed job without skipping adjacent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forward `forEach` shifts the next job into the already-visited index. For `[done, done]`, the first splice leaves the second job at index 0 and it remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Preserve pruneDone's non-mutating API behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation returned a filtered copy; this version removes items from the caller-owned array. Existing callers that retain `jobs` for persistence, retry, or reporting will unexpectedly lose completed jobs.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average result
findings.whyItBreaks: For `averageAmount([])`, the reducer returns 0 and division by `rows.length` (0) produces NaN. This regresses the prior public behavior of returning 0 for a valid empty `Row[]`.

findings.title: Avoid sorting the caller's rows in place
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.prototype.sort` mutates `rows`, whereas the previous implementation sorted a copy. Callers that retain the input now observe its order changed merely by asking for the busiest row.

findings.title: Restore the empty-input guard
findings.whyItBreaks: For averageAmount([]), total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this returns NaN instead of the prior numeric fallback 0.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's row order
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates `rows`; callers that reuse the input after calling busiest now observe it reordered by amount, unlike the prior defensive-copy behavior.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average
findings.whyItBreaks: For averageAmount([]), total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so the function now returns NaN instead of its previous 0 result. Consumers receiving this public numeric result can propagate NaN into totals, displays, or persisted calculations.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller’s rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows in place. This changes busiest() from a read-only lookup into an operation that silently reorders the caller’s input, breaking callers that retain rows in their original order.

findings.title: Restore numeric score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Default Array.sort compares scores as strings. For players ordered as score 9 then 100 with n=1, ranking becomes [9,100], cutoff is 9, and slice returns the 9-point player rather than the 100-point player.

findings.title: Restore numeric ordering for score cutoffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For scores [100, 9, 99] and n=2, rankScores returns [99, 9, 100], setting the cutoff to 9; topPlayers then returns the first two original players and can omit the 99-point player.

findings.title: Restore numeric descending score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. With players ordered as score 2 then 10 and n=1, rankScores returns [2, 10], producing a cutoff of 2; topPlayers then returns the score-2 player instead of the score-10 player.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `==` to compare attacker-controlled signatures can leak how much of the expected HMAC matches through comparison timing. A remote attacker can use repeated requests to incrementally forge a signature accepted by the webhook processor.

findings.title: Restore constant-time webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Direct string equality can short-circuit based on the matching prefix, exposing a timing side channel for attacker-controlled webhook signatures. The previous hmac.compare_digest implementation was specifically timing-safe.

findings.title: Restore constant-time webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: String equality can stop at the first differing character, allowing a requester to use response timing to learn the expected HMAC incrementally. A forged signature can then pass the authentication gate and invoke processor(payload).

findings.title: Keep balance updates in the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the context at lines 22-23 exits. If either balance update then raises, the transfer returns an error but the ledger row remains committed; a failure between the two updates can also leave only one balance changed. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep balance updates in the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the transaction block exits before either balance update runs. If either subsequent update fails, the transfer raises after recording a completed ledger entry; if the second update fails, the source debit can also persist without the destination credit.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits immediately after the ledger insert, before either balance update. If either subsequent UPDATE fails, the ledger entry remains committed; if the second fails, the source debit may also remain without a destination credit. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep billing-day calculation in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: This changes the established UTC billing key to the server's local calendar date. For example, with TZ=America/Los_Angeles, new Date("2026-01-01T00:30:00Z") now returns "2025-12-31" rather than the previous "2026-01-01", so identical instants can be assigned to different billing days across deployments or after a timezone configuration change.

findings.title: Keep billing days in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: This replaces UTC accessors with local-time accessors. For example, under America/Los_Angeles, the instant 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z now produces 2025-12-31 rather than 2026-01-01. Billing classification and sameBillingDay therefore vary with the server's configured timezone.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing date
findings.whyItBreaks: A UTC instant now maps to different billing days depending on the process timezone. For example, in America/Los_Angeles, 2026-01-01T00:30:00.000Z returns 2025-12-31 instead of the prior 2026-01-01, so sameBillingDay can also classify identical UTC billing periods differently across deployments.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two requests for the same account in different tenants now share one memo entry. After tenant A caches account X, reading account X for tenant B returns tenant A's Profile without invoking fetchProfile, producing incorrect cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Include tenant in the memo key
findings.whyItBreaks: After `readProfile("tenant-a", "alice", ...)` caches tenant A's profile, `readProfile("tenant-b", "alice", ...)` returns that cached profile at line 16 without calling `fetchProfile`. This leaks cross-tenant profile data and reports the wrong tenant.

findings.title: Include tenant in the memoization key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A caches account `alice`, a read for tenant B and account `alice` hits the same `memo` entry at line 15 and returns tenant A's Profile without calling fetchProfile. This exposes incorrect cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `Error("missing: ...")`; it now returns `""`, which is a valid stored value. Callers, including `loadAll`, can no longer distinguish absent data from an intentionally empty value and may proceed with incomplete data.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key failures
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw, including through loadAll. It now returns "", which is indistinguishable from a key legitimately stored with an empty-string value; loadAll therefore returns a successful-looking value for missing entries.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `Error("missing: <key>")`; this exported function now returns `""`, indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty string. `loadAll` consequently returns partial-looking data such as `["value", ""]` instead of reporting a missing required key.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility with the existing Config fields
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing callers pass the exported `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` shape. They now fail TypeScript validation because `retries` and `timeout` are required. Untyped existing callers get `config.timeout === undefined`, so `Date.now() + undefined` is NaN and the deadline guard never stops retries.

findings.title: Make retryBackground actually run in the background
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported name promises background execution, but the implementation invokes `fn()` synchronously before returning. A blocking or slow callback blocks the caller just as `retry` does, so this API provides no background behavior and can unexpectedly stall its caller.

findings.title: Expose retryBackground terminal failures to callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from `fn` is discarded and exhaustion of retries or timeout also returns indistinguishable `void`. Because this is an exported API, callers cannot distinguish a successful background retry from a failed one and may treat failed work as complete.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config input contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing callers construct Config with timeoutMs and no retries. TypeScript consumers no longer compile; transpiled JavaScript consumers produce Date.now() + undefined, making the deadline NaN so retry's timeout guard never fires.

findings.title: Surface background retry exhaustion
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground catches every callback exception and returns void after exhausting retries or timing out. Its public callers cannot distinguish a successful callback from total failure, so they can continue as if work completed.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config timeout contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers supplying the former `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` shape no longer type-check because `timeoutMs` was removed and `retries` is newly required. Existing JavaScript callers instead produce `deadline = NaN`; both deadline guards evaluate false, so the configured timeout no longer stops retries.

findings.title: Run retryBackground outside the caller's execution path
findings.whyItBreaks: `retryBackground` directly invokes `fn()` and executes its entire retry loop before returning. Its public name promises background execution, but a slow or repeatedly failing function blocks the caller exactly like `retry` does.

findings.title: Expose failure after background retries are exhausted
findings.whyItBreaks: When every invocation throws, the catch discards every exception and the function falls through with the same `void` return as a successful retry. Callers cannot distinguish an exhausted failure from success.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now accepts number, but number has no length property. TypeScript compilation fails for this expression; if transpiled without type-checking, <Field value={42} /> renders "len=undefined" instead of a valid numeric label.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `value` now publicly accepts a number, but `value.length` only exists on strings. `<Field value={12} />` fails TypeScript checking; if emitted despite that error, it renders `len=undefined` rather than the digit length.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `value` now has type `string | number`, so TypeScript rejects `value.length` because numbers have no `length`. If emitted without type checking, `<Field value={42} />` renders `len=undefined`.

findings.title: Restore the buffer for large diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer lowers spawnSync's captured-output limit from 64 MiB to Node's 1 MiB default. The same helper captures the complete `git diff` patch at line 140; patches above that limit cause spawnSync to fail, which reaches runGithub's catch path and posts a failed review check instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Restore a sufficient Git output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, spawnSync defaults stdout/stderr to 1 MiB. A PR whose `git diff` at line 140 exceeds that limit has its Git process terminated; line 39 throws before the error-handling block at line 175, so no review or failure check is posted.

findings.title: Restore the Git diff buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, Node spawnSync defaults to 1,048,576 bytes and terminates a child whose stdout exceeds it. git() then sees a nonzero/null status and throws, so a PR with a diff over 1 MiB reaches runGithub's failure handler instead of posting its review.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox override
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex now invokes Codex without a sandbox policy. On runners whose ambient Codex configuration permits workspace writes, a prompt can modify opts.repoPath; the previous '-s read-only' override prevented those writes regardless of ambient configuration.

findings.title: Keep the Codex subprocess read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` causes this exported function to inherit Codex's configured sandbox policy. A host configured for `workspace-write` can now let the model execute prompt-directed writes in `opts.repoPath`; previously the explicit CLI option prevented those writes regardless of user configuration.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox for review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` lets the configured/default Codex sandbox policy apply. Since the process runs with `cwd: opts.repoPath` and sends the review prompt to an agent capable of executing commands, a writable policy can now let a review modify the repository it is meant to inspect.

findings.title: Diff the configured PR revisions via their merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA may be a newer base-branch tip that is not an ancestor of the PR head. Diffing it directly against HEAD includes base-only commits as apparent PR changes, so the bundle can review and classify files the PR did not change. This also ignores PR_HEAD_SHA for the patch while checks and review publication remain tied to headSha.

findings.title: Diff from the merge base to the PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current target-branch tip and that branch has advanced since the PR branched, it is not an ancestor of the PR head. `git diff baseSha HEAD` then includes target-branch-only changes as reversions. The review receives those unrelated files in both `patch` and `changedFiles`, but posts its review against `headSha` at lines 178-179, allowing false findings/comments on a different commit's changes.

findings.title: Diff from the PR merge-base to the resolved head
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current target-branch tip and that branch advanced after the PR forked, it is not necessarily an ancestor of the PR head. `git diff baseSha HEAD` then includes target-only edits as removals/changes, so the bundle given to `review` can report or block the PR for code the PR did not change. The removed merge-base computation selected the PR's actual comparison point.

findings.title: Use headSha for the bundle's compared revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The bundle declares `headSha` from PR_HEAD_SHA, and reviews/checks are posted to that SHA, but the changed patch and paths now end at the checkout's `HEAD`. If the checkout is a merge ref or stale while PR_HEAD_SHA identifies the PR commit, Needlefish analyzes one revision and attaches its result to another; inline findings can be invalid for the posted commit.

findings.title: Preserve prompt replacement strings literally
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets $-tokens in a string replacement. A patch or serialized finding containing `$&` is inserted as the template marker rather than literal source text; `$`` and `$'` similarly splice template content. Since bundle.patch and model-produced findings are prompt data, either review stage can receive a corrupted prompt and fail to review the actual change.

findings.title: Preserve literal text when expanding prompt placeholders
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets `$&`, `$'`, `$`` and `$$` in a string replacement. A reviewed patch or serialized bundle containing `$&` is changed to the placeholder text, while `$'` or `$`` injects prompt suffix/prefix text into the interpolated input. This corrupts the prompt passed to the reviewer/critic and can produce an incorrect verdict for otherwise valid source content.

findings.title: Keep prompt payloads literal during replacement
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace treats $&, $`, $', and $$ specially when its replacement is a string. A diff, bundle field, or candidate finding containing (for example) "$&" is rewritten to the matched placeholder rather than preserved literally; "$`" can insert the entire prompt prefix. This corrupts the review context or critic patch and can cause incorrect review results for otherwise valid source changes.

findings.title: Keep fallback reviews pinned to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub snapshots headSha and computes the reviewed patch from it before awaiting review. If the first review POST fails and a new commit is pushed before this fallback runs, omitting commit_id makes GitHub attach the fallback review to the PR's then-current head instead. The review body can therefore report findings for SHA A as though it reviewed newer SHA B.

findings.title: Preserve the reviewed commit in the fallback request
findings.whyItBreaks: The review result is computed for headSha (captured at src/adapters/github.ts:141 and used for the diff at lines 143-145). When the primary request fails—commonly because an inline comment is rejected—the fallback now omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit. If the PR is updated during review, a REQUEST_CHANGES result for the older analyzed SHA is posted against the new SHA and can incorrectly block it.

findings.title: Retain the reviewed SHA in the fallback POST
findings.whyItBreaks: The review result is computed from `headSha`, but this fallback now omits that SHA. GitHub defaults an omitted `commit_id` to the PR's most recent commit. If the PR advances after the review snapshot is computed and the initial inline-comment request fails, a stale REQUEST_CHANGES or COMMENT review is attached to the newer, unreviewed commit.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid review entries now become P1/bug findings with an empty file and line 0 instead of signaling malformed output. For example, an entry without file or lineStart is returned as a Finding targeting "" at 0, which callers cannot distinguish from a genuine finding.

findings.title: Preserve the exported strict normalization mode
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported strict parameter breaks TypeScript callers that pass it. At runtime, callers that previously used strict=false to omit malformed entries now receive fabricated default findings because the function always maps every entry.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating P1 reports
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid required fields now become a valid-looking Finding (for example, invalid severity becomes P1 while missing file and lineStart become "" and 0). Callers can no longer distinguish malformed review output from a real finding, whereas this path previously threw a malformed-finding error.

findings.title: Preserve the strict parameter's two normalization modes
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers of normalizeReview(review, false) no longer compile. JavaScript callers silently receive different data: malformed findings that were previously filtered in non-strict mode are now retained as defaulted findings.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid review output now succeeds as a Finding: for example, an unsupported severity becomes P1, a missing file becomes an empty string, and missing line numbers become 0. Previously these inputs threw validation errors. normalizeReview at line 131 therefore returns a result whose caller cannot distinguish malformed model output from a legitimate finding.

findings.title: Restore an explicit repository for manual ref resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: `workflow_dispatch` has no pull_request payload, so this path runs before any checkout. Without `-R "$REPO"` (or `GH_REPO`), `gh pr view` must infer a repository from a local Git remote; a fresh self-hosted runner workspace has none. The failed substitutions write empty `head` and `base` outputs, so the following checkout cannot target the requested PR.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before actions/checkout. Without -R (or GH_REPO), gh pr view must infer its repository from a local Git repository; a clean runner workspace has not been checked out yet. The PR lookup therefore fails and emits empty head/base outputs, preventing the requested PR head from being checked out.

findings.title: Keep an explicit repository for manual PR ref resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so these commands run before the first actions/checkout step. Without -R "$REPO", gh pr view has no repository context to resolve PR_NUM against, causing ref resolution to fail (or depend on stale self-hosted runner state) and preventing the requested PR checkout.

findings.title: Preserve malformed review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs that previously threw explicit malformed-review errors now return a valid-looking empty review. Callers of this exported API cannot distinguish an invalid provider response from an actual review with no findings, so they can report or persist a false clean result.

findings.title: Reject malformed review envelopes
findings.whyItBreaks: Missing or wrongly typed required fields now become empty strings or arrays. A truncated/malformed review therefore becomes indistinguishable from a legitimate review with no findings or blocking residual risks, whereas the previous implementation propagated a malformed-output error.

findings.title: Reject malformed review envelopes
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as null, {}, or a response missing required arrays now return { summary: "", findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: [] }, which is also a legitimate empty review shape. Callers of this exported API can no longer distinguish malformed provider output from a successful review with no findings.

findings.title: Resolve selected PR refs for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: A `workflow_dispatch` event has no `pull_request` payload, so this falls back to `github.ref` rather than the head of the PR supplied in `pr_number`. The review therefore checks out the branch/tag used to start the workflow (normally the default branch), while PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA are also empty at lines 45-46. Manual review of a selected PR no longer runs against that PR's code or diff.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, the event has no pull_request payload. Therefore the checkout expression falls back to github.ref (the branch selected when starting the workflow, not the required pr_number's head), while PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA are both empty. Previously this path queried gh pr view using pr_number and used the resolved head/base for checkout and review. Manual reviews now run the repository version selected at dispatch and lack the requested PR revision pair.

findings.title: Resolve requested PR refs in manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The checkout therefore uses github.ref (the branch selected to run the workflow, commonly main), and the base fetch defaults to main, rather than the PR identified by pr_number. The self-review consequently runs the tool from an unrelated revision; PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA are also empty on the subsequent review step.

findings.title: Restore the git diff buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses its 1 MiB default. runLocal passes the unbounded output of `git diff baseSha HEAD` at line 100 through this wrapper, so a 1–64 MiB diff now terminates with a max-buffer error (and this code throws) instead of being reviewed as it was before this change.

findings.title: Retain sufficient buffer space for git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer changes spawnSync's stdout limit from 64 MiB to Node's 1 MiB default. runLocal reads the complete raw git diff through this wrapper; a diff over 1 MiB causes spawnSync to terminate with a buffer error/status null, and line 12 throws instead of producing a review.

findings.title: Restore the Git diff output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer changes spawnSync from the previous 64 MiB limit to Node's 1 MiB default. runLocal obtains the complete review patch through git diff at line 100, so a 1–64 MiB diff now exceeds the buffer, causes git() to throw, and produces no review.

findings.title: Report failed reviews as failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When review(), review posting, or successful-check posting throws, this catch path creates the required "Needlefish" check with conclusion "neutral". GitHub treats neutral as a successful required-check status, so a PR can be merged even though the review explicitly failed and this process exits nonzero. [GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches)

findings.title: Keep review errors failing
findings.whyItBreaks: When reviewing or posting a review throws, this reports the named Needlefish check as neutral. GitHub treats neutral as a successful required-check conclusion, so branch protection can permit merging even though the review produced no verdict.

findings.title: Keep review errors as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: A thrown review now posts a completed neutral Check Run. GitHub accepts neutral conclusions for required status checks, so a repository requiring the Needlefish check can merge even though the review errored and produced no verdict.

findings.title: Scope the PR diff command to the configured repository
findings.whyItBreaks: gh pr diff resolves its repository from the process working directory, while this adapter identifies the target with GITHUB_REPOSITORY and accepts a separate cwd. When those differ, the command can fail or fetch the same-numbered PR from another repository, causing the review patch to disagree with the metadata and local changed-file set.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The job checks out the PR head into the workspace and invokes `src/cli.ts` from that checkout. A same-repository PR can add or alter that file (or package lifecycle scripts) to forge a review result or execute arbitrary code while `GH_TOKEN` has `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write` permissions on a self-hosted runner.

findings.title: Restore checkout of the reviewer package
findings.whyItBreaks: This repository's head contains only `.github/workflows/review.yml` and `.needlefish/answers.json`; it has no `package.json`, lockfile, `node_modules`, or `src/cli.ts`. Consequently `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` cannot install a package in the workspace, and the later `tsx src/cli.ts` invocation cannot exist. Every review workflow run fails before producing a review.

findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head is now the workspace root, then its dependency configuration and src/cli.ts are installed and executed. A same-repository PR can therefore alter the reviewer code that runs on the self-hosted runner with a GITHUB_TOKEN granted pull-request and check write permissions, allowing it to forge review/check output or compromise the runner. The removed separate main checkout prevented this.

findings.title: Restore a checkout that contains the reviewer package
findings.whyItBreaks: Both reviewed commit trees contain only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json: there is no package.json or src/cli.ts. Consequently pnpm install cannot locate a project manifest and the subsequent CLI path does not exist, so no review job can complete after this workflow is merged.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The root checkout is the PR head, so this command executes that PR's src/cli.ts rather than an independently trusted reviewer. An internal PR can alter the CLI to report success or suppress findings. The preceding install also resolves the PR-controlled manifest on a self-hosted runner, enabling arbitrary install-time code execution.

The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Preserve case-insensitive severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously converted values such as " p1 " and "p1" to the valid severity "P1". The new membership check compares the raw value directly, so those inputs now fall back to "P3", silently downgrading findings supplied through this exported normalization boundary.

findings.title: Preserve severity canonicalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped raw findings and routes each through this function. Previously " p0 " and "p0" normalized to P0; they now fail the exact-match check and become P3, incorrectly downgrading real critical findings.

findings.title: Canonicalize severity before membership check
findings.whyItBreaks: `normalizeReview` accepts untyped parsed input and calls this function. A valid severity such as `" p0 "` or `"p0"`, previously normalized to `P0`, now fails the exact-membership check and is returned as `P3`, incorrectly downgrading a critical finding.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env object, spawnSync inherits process.env, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. The invoked Codex agent can read its environment while reviewing repository-controlled content, allowing prompt injection or tool output to exfiltrate the caller's GitHub credential. The base revision explicitly removed these variables before launching Codex.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the agent child
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting spawnSync's env option causes the Codex process to inherit process.env, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. The prior implementation deliberately removed these credentials before passing an arbitrary prompt to an agent capable of inspecting repository content and returning command output; prompt-injected instructions can now read and disclose or use the runner's GitHub credential.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting `env` makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`. Consequently, `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN` are available to the spawned Codex process, which receives the supplied prompt and can expose the credentials through its command or model output. The base implementation explicitly stripped these secrets.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard before executing PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs now reach a self-hosted runner, check out their head SHA, install their dependency graph, and execute their modified TypeScript via tsx. An attacker can submit a fork PR to run arbitrary code in the runner environment, potentially accessing runner credentials, workspace data, or network resources.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard for this self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs now reach checkout, dependency installation, and execution of the PR-controlled CLI on a persistent self-hosted runner. An attacker can modify the checked-out code or dependency metadata to execute arbitrary commands and access or persist on the runner.

findings.title: Restore the fork trust boundary for the self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork pull requests now reach a self-hosted runner, checkout their exact head SHA, install their dependency graph, and execute their modified CLI. A contributor can alter the checked-out code or package scripts to execute arbitrary commands in the runner's security context and access/exfiltrate anything available to that runner.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration configuration values
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous parser accepted 0, allowing operators to configure immediate SIGKILL or immediate post-SIGKILL completion. Now "0" falls back to 5000 ms for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS and 2000 ms for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS, silently changing configured timeout behavior.

findings.title: Keep zero-valued runner delays valid
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version accepts "0". This change maps it to the fallback instead: NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 now waits 5000ms before SIGKILL, and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now waits 2000ms before resolving, rather than honoring the configured immediate delay.

findings.title: Preserve zero as a valid runner timing configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: An explicit value of `0` previously configured no grace period. It now fails the new predicate and silently becomes the 5000 ms timeout grace or 2000 ms SIGKILL give-up delay. In particular, `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` now waits five seconds before SIGKILL instead of escalating immediately, breaking existing configuration and delaying timed-out runner cleanup.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from deep reviewers
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep review can return a blocking residual risk, but candidateMerged now always serializes residual_risks as []. The critic therefore cannot distinguish a fully reviewed patch from one with unresolved blocking evidence, and may emit a non-blocking verdict.

findings.title: Restore deep coverage for unselected changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews retain only six mapped hotspots. With the coverage backstop removed, any changed file absent from those six is never sent to a deep review; its defects cannot enter the merged candidate.

findings.title: Keep the explanation in the finding deduplication key
findings.whyItBreaks: Distinct findings at the same file, line, and category now collapse whenever their normalized titles share the first 60 characters, even if their whyItBreaks values describe different defects. One real finding is then omitted from the review result.

findings.title: Preserve distinct findings during deduplication
findings.whyItBreaks: Two distinct findings at the same file, line, and category that share the first 60 characters of their titles now overwrite one another even when their whyItBreaks values describe separate defects. The former key retained that distinction, so an independent finding can silently disappear from the final review.

findings.title: Deep-review every changed file
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews process only the six selected hotspots. A map response with more than six hotspots, or one that omits a changed path, leaves those files out of every deep-review call. The removed tail hotspot previously covered all such paths; the critic receives only patchStat on this path, so the omitted diff is not supplied for a compensating review.

findings.title: Return a blocking review when one deep pass fails
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed or failed Codex response for any one hotspot now rejects the entire exported review() call, skipping the remaining hotspots and critic pass. Previously this failure was converted into a blocking residual risk while preserving completed work, so consumers received a structured ReviewResult instead of losing the review.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual risks to the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: A successful deep pass can report a blocking residual risk, but this path now replaces every such signal with []. The critic therefore receives identical input for an incomplete deep review and a clean one, and cannot preserve the prior blocker in its output.

findings.title: Restore coverage for every changed file
findings.whyItBreaks: Large bundles select at most six hotspots. Removing the tail hotspot means any file omitted by the mapper, or assigned only to a seventh hotspot, never reaches the deep-review loop. The resulting candidate contains no review evidence for that file, so a defect confined to it can be silently omitted.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass can return a blocking residual risk, but this now replaces all of them with an empty list before the critic sees the merged review. The specific unresolved condition is therefore lost and cannot be represented in the final ReviewResult, allowing an incomplete large review to be treated as complete.

findings.title: Forward focus and deep options through large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Requests crossing the large-review threshold no longer pass `bundle.focus` or `bundle.deep` to the map prompt, and `focus` is also no longer substituted into each deep-review prompt. The same options remain included for small reviews, so a caller's requested review scope/depth is silently ignored only for patches over 30,000 characters or 10 files.

findings.title: Restore focus propagation for large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: For bundles over the large-review threshold, the deep-review prompt no longer replaces {{FOCUS}} with bundle.focus. The prompt therefore receives the literal token instead of the requested review scope; small reviews still serialize the whole bundle, so focus now works only for small PRs. The map pass also no longer receives focus, so hotspot selection cannot prioritize it.

findings.title: Restore focus propagation for large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewSmall serializes the entire Bundle, but reviewLarge now omits bundle.focus from both its map input and each deep-review prompt. A caller requesting a focused review therefore gets that request ignored whenever the patch crosses the large-review threshold.

findings.title: Normalize seconds after rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: Rounding only the post-modulo remainder can produce a 60-second component without carrying it into minutes. For example, 119500 ms renders as `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`, affecting both per-call and total duration output.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For values from 59.5 to under 60 seconds within a minute, such as 59950ms, this computes 0m 60s (or 9m 60s for 599950ms) instead of carrying the rounded second into the minute. The rendered per-call and total durations therefore display an invalid and incorrect time.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the minute component
findings.whyItBreaks: For ms=119500, minutes is 1 and seconds rounds to 60, so the report renders "1m 60s" rather than "2m 0s". This affects both individual call durations and the rendered total.

findings.title: Reject zero to honor the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger and its error text promise a positive integer, but the changed predicate accepts "0" and returns 0. As an exported parser, callers can now receive a value outside the promised domain and skip their own validation.

findings.title: Reject zero to preserve the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns `0`, although both its exported name and error contract promise a positive integer. Public callers can therefore receive an invalid zero value while relying on the advertised validation.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The public function and its error text promise a positive integer, but input "0" now returns 0. External callers relying on this parser to validate strictly positive capacities, counts, or limits will receive an invalid zero without an error.
